claim: Most human aneuploidies originate maternally.
source: Most human aneuploidies originate maternally.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the origin of human aneuploidies.

claim: Male sterility is common among aneuploid mice used to study chromosomal abnormalities.
source: Indeed, male sterility is common among aneuploid mice used to study chromosomal abnormalities, and male germline transmission of exogenous DNA has been rarely reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to existing literature and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Male germline transmission of exogenous DNA has been rarely reported.
source: Indeed, male sterility is common among aneuploid mice used to study chromosomal abnormalities, and male germline transmission of exogenous DNA has been rarely reported.
evidence: This is supported by references to existing literature in the field.

claim: Males of the aneuploid Tc1 mouse strain produce viable sperm despite aberrant testis architecture.
source: Here we show that, despite aberrant testis architecture, males of the aneuploid Tc1 mouse strain produce viable sperm and transmit human chromosome 21 to create aneuploid offspring.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript, including histological analysis and breeding experiments.

claim: Tc1 males transmit human chromosome 21 to create aneuploid offspring.
source: Here we show that, despite aberrant testis architecture, males of the aneuploid Tc1 mouse strain produce viable sperm and transmit human chromosome 21 to create aneuploid offspring.
evidence: This is supported by breeding experiments and genotyping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chromatin condensation during spermatogenesis and extensive epigenetic reprogramming specific to male germline transmission resulted in almost indistinguishable patterns of transcriptional deployment compared to female passage.
source: Remarkably, when compared with mice derived from female passage of human chromosome 21, the chromatin condensation during spermatogenesis and the extensive epigenetic reprogramming specific to male germline transmission resulted in almost indistinguishable patterns of transcriptional deployment.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq, RNA-Seq, and other epigenetic profiling data comparing male and female germline-derived offspring.

claim: Down Syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 that is maternally inherited in over 90% of all cases.
source: The most common viable aneuploidy in humans is Down Syndrome, which is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 that is maternally inherited in over 90% of all cases (Hultén et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hultén et al., 2010.

claim: The Tc1 mouse transmits an almost complete copy of human chromosome 21 via the female germline.
source: An elegant mouse model of human Down Syndrome is the aneuploid Tc1 mouse, which transmits an almost complete copy of human chromosome 21 (HsChr21) via the female germline (O'Doherty et al., 2005; Sheppard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Doherty et al., 2005 and Sheppard et al., 2012.

claim: Most trisomic mouse models exhibit total male sterility.
source: More generally, passage of aneuploid DNA via the female germline is preferred in the majority of trisomic mouse models, most of which exhibit total male sterility (Davisson et al., 2007; Hernandez and Fisher, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davisson et al., 2007 and Hernandez and Fisher, 1999.

claim: Efficient and stable male germline transmission of foreign aneuploid DNA has only been reported in mice for comparatively small human artificial or fragmented chromosomes.
source: Across mammals, efficient and stable male germline transmission of foreign aneuploid DNA has only been reported in mice for comparatively small human artificial or fragmented chromosomes (Tomizuka et al., 1997; Voet et al., 2001; Weuts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomizuka et al., 1997; Voet et al., 2001; and Weuts et al., 2012.

claim: Female meiosis can extend over decades and is thus more error-prone than male meiosis.
source: The mechanisms of mammalian gametogenesis disfavour paternally-derived aneuploidies as a result of sexual dimorphism in meiosis: female meiosis can extend over decades and is thus more error-prone, whereas male meiosis is a continuous process with stringent quality checkpoints (Hunt and Hassold, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hunt and Hassold, 2002.

claim: Male meiosis is a continuous process with stringent quality checkpoints.
source: The mechanisms of mammalian gametogenesis disfavour paternally-derived aneuploidies as a result of sexual dimorphism in meiosis: female meiosis can extend over decades and is thus more error-prone, whereas male meiosis is a continuous process with stringent quality checkpoints (Hunt and Hassold, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hunt and Hassold, 2002.

claim: Human oocytes show 20% occurrence of chromosomal abnormalities.
source: Indeed, human gametes show an order of magnitude difference in the occurrence of chromosomal abnormalities between oocytes (20%) and sperm (2–4%) (Martin et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martin et al., 1991.

claim: Human sperm show 2-4% occurrence of chromosomal abnormalities.
source: Indeed, human gametes show an order of magnitude difference in the occurrence of chromosomal abnormalities between oocytes (20%) and sperm (2–4%) (Martin et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martin et al., 1991.

claim: The maternally passaged haploid genome remains histone-bound throughout gametogenesis, fertilization, and zygotic activation.
source: Throughout this process, the maternally passaged haploid genome remains histone-bound (Cantone and Fisher, 2013; Kimmins and Sassone-Corsi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cantone and Fisher, 2013 and Kimmins and Sassone-Corsi, 2005.

claim: Spermatogenesis results in DNA that is 6-20 times more compact than histone-bound DNA.
source: In stark contrast, spermatogenesis results in a form of DNA that is 6–20 times more compact than histone-bound DNA (Balhorn, 2007; Dadoune, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Balhorn, 2007 and Dadoune, 1995.

claim: DNA compaction during spermatogenesis is achieved by replacing histone proteins with sperm-specific protamine proteins.
source: This compaction is achieved by replacing histone proteins with sperm-specific protamine proteins, leaving very few histones bound to DNA (Brykczynska et al., 2010; Erkek et al., 2013; Hammoud et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brykczynska et al., 2010; Erkek et al., 2013; and Hammoud et al., 2009.

claim: Sperm development is associated with massive and genome-wide derepression of transcription.
source: Sperm development is associated with massive and genome-wide derepression of transcription (Soumillon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soumillon et al., 2013.

claim: During male meiosis, almost all genes and otherwise-silenced repeat elements are expressed at extremely high levels.
source: During male meiosis, almost all genes, as well as otherwise-silenced repeat elements, are expressed at extremely high levels (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ward et al., 2013.

claim: Tc1 males showed significantly decreased testis size and weight compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Tc1 males showed significantly decreased testis size and weight, as well as markedly decreased sperm count (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Tc1 males showed markedly decreased sperm count compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Tc1 males showed significantly decreased testis size and weight, as well as markedly decreased sperm count (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Total body weight and liver weight were indistinguishable between Tc1 and Tc0 mice.
source: Tc1-associated phenotypes appeared to be specific to testes, as total body weight and liver weight (as a representative somatic tissue) were indistinguishable between Tc1 and Tc0 mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tc1 testes showed subfertility phenotypes characterized by the absence or reduced frequency of secondary spermatocytes.
source: The Tc1 males' subfertility phenotype was characterized by the absence (spermatogenic arrest) or reduced frequency (hypo-spermatogenesis) of secondary spermatocytes, as well as the absence of any cell types derived from these (Figure 1C) (Borg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1C and cited reference to Borg et al., 2010.

claim: Neither Tc1 nor Tc0 mice demonstrated Sertoli cell-only syndrome, tubular sclerosis, or fibrosis.
source: Neither Tc1 nor Tc0 mice demonstrated other subfertility phenotypes, such as Sertoli cell-only syndrome, tubular sclerosis, or fibrosis (Dohle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on histological observations and cited reference to Dohle et al., 2012.

claim: Defective tubules in Tc1 males often displayed failures in chromosome segregation during metaphase of meiosis I.
source: Interestingly, while defective tubules in wild-types mainly displayed an absence of mature sperm, defective tubules in Tc1 males often displayed failures in chromosome segregation during metaphase of meiosis I (Figure 1C, red arrowheads and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tc1 mice show a wider and more diffuse distribution of γH2AFX that does not appear to be restricted to leptotene cells.
source: In contrast, Tc1 mice show a wider and more diffuse distribution of γH2AFX that does not appear to be restricted to leptotene cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Tc1 males display a subfertility phenotype but produce mature spermatozoa in a substantial subset of seminiferous tubules.
source: In sum, Tc1 males display a subfertility phenotype but produce mature spermatozoa in a substantial subset of seminiferous tubules.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the histological data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: There is a significant increase in the percentage of stage XII tubules in Tc1 males, supporting an arrest at metaphase I.
source: This classification revealed a significant increase in the percentage of stage XII tubules in Tc1 males, supporting an arrest at metaphase I (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of seminiferous tubule stages shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Quantification revealed a significant increase in the percentage of primary spermatocytes in Tc1 animals over wild-types.
source: Quantification revealed a significant increase in the percentage of primary spermatocytes in Tc1 animals over wild-types and a corresponding decrease in both round and elongating spermatids.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data using ilastik.

claim: There is a corresponding decrease in both round and elongating spermatids in Tc1 animals compared to wild-types.
source: Quantification revealed a significant increase in the percentage of primary spermatocytes in Tc1 animals over wild-types and a corresponding decrease in both round and elongating spermatids.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data using ilastik.

claim: The percentage of meiotic cells was almost twice as high in Tc1 animals compared to wild-types.
source: Meiotic cells have a high level of pH3 staining, a histone modification commonly found on metaphase chromosomes (Wei et al., 1999); on average, the percentage of meiotic cells was almost twice as high in Tc1 animals.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of pH3-positive cells and cited reference to Wei et al., 1999.

claim: There is an almost 2-fold increase in the ratio of metaphase I to pro-metaphase cells in Tc1 males compared to wild-types.
source: Despite variability especially amongst Tc1 animals, we observe an almost 2-fold increase in the ratio of metaphase I to pro-metaphase cells (1.02 for Tc1 and 0.52 for Tc0), supporting an arrest at metaphase I.
evidence: This is based on manual classification of meiotic cells from immunofluorescence data.

claim: Abnormal metaphase cells with congression defects were observed more frequently in Tc1 males compared to wild-types.
source: Interestingly, we observed abnormal metaphase cells with congression defects more frequently in Tc1 males compared to wild-types, which may contribute to the metaphase I arrest (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on observations from immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There is a drastic increase in the percentage of cells displaying positive staining for cleaved caspase-3 within stage XII tubules of Tc1 males.
source: Finally, we observed a drastic increase in the percentage of cells displaying positive staining for cleaved caspase-3 within stage XII tubules of Tc1 males (Figure 2F), consistent with increased apoptosis due to the activation of the spindle checkpoint at metaphase I (Eaker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2F and cited reference to Eaker et al., 2001.

claim: Spermatogenesis in Tc1 males is impaired primarily at epithelial stage XII due to the activation of the spindle checkpoint at metaphase I.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate that spermatogenesis in Tc1 males is impaired primarily at epithelial stage XII due to the activation of the spindle checkpoint at metaphase I.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: Successful transmission of human chromosome 21 occurs in 35% of offspring born to aneuploid Tc1 mothers.
source: We first confirmed that successful transmission of human chromosome 21 occurs in 35% of offspring born to aneuploid Tc1 mothers (O'Doherty et al., 2005) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by breeding data and cited reference to O'Doherty et al., 2005.

claim: 38 actively breeding Tc1 female mice produced 824 offspring in 153 litters, 290 of which were Tc1 positive.
source: We produced 824 offspring in 153 litters from 38 actively breeding Tc1 female mice, 290 of these offspring were Tc1 positive (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is breeding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Breeding experiments with aneuploid Tc1 males produced successful transmission of human chromosome 21 in 11% of offspring born to wild-type mothers.
source: Remarkably, parallel breeding experiments with aneuploid Tc1 males, where the human chromosome is passaged via sperm, produced successful transmission of human chromosome 21 in 11% of offspring born to wild-type mothers.
evidence: This is breeding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Twenty-seven breeding Tc1 males produced 138 litters with a total of 910 offspring, 98 of which were Tc1 positive.
source: Twenty-seven breeding Tc1 males produced 138 litters with a total of 910 offspring, 98 of which were Tc1 positive.
evidence: This is breeding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Male germline-derived offspring are macroscopically indistinguishable from female germline-derived offspring.
source: Male germline-derived offspring are macroscopically indistinguishable from female germline-derived offspring and no novel histological alterations were identified across different tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No novel histological alterations were identified across different tissues in male germline-derived offspring compared to female germline-derived offspring.
source: Male germline-derived offspring are macroscopically indistinguishable from female germline-derived offspring and no novel histological alterations were identified across different tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of Tc1 males used for breeding (21 out of 27) were fertile.
source: Despite the subfertility phenotypes we observed for Tc1 males, the majority of males used for breeding (21 out of 27) were fertile.
evidence: This is based on breeding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 19 out of 21 fertile Tc1 breeders transmitted human chromosome 21 at least once to their offspring.
source: 19 out of these 21 breeders transmitted human chromosome 21 at least once to their offspring, with individual breeders showing varying transmission rates and inconsistent litter frequencies (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on breeding data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Male germline-derived offspring are themselves fertile and can successfully transmit human chromosome 21.
source: Male germline-derived offspring are themselves fertile and can successfully transmit human chromosome 21.
evidence: This is based on breeding experiments with male germline-derived offspring.

claim: Almost all of the 4N spermatocytes (~94%) were positive for HsChr21.
source: Almost all of the 4N spermatocytes (~94%) were positive for HsChr21, showing a surprisingly low level of mosaicism compared to previously published rates in somatic tissues (O'Doherty et al., 2005; Wilson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis of sorted spermatocytes and cited references to O'Doherty et al., 2005 and Wilson et al., 2008.

claim: Approximately 34% of round and elongating spermatids carried HsChr21.
source: Among the haploid population, approximately 34% of round and elongating spermatids carried HsChr21.
evidence: This is based on FISH analysis of sorted spermatids.

claim: The mouse male germline can successfully package an exogenous and aneuploid 42 MB human chromosome into protamines to generate reproductively active sperm.
source: Although occurring at an appreciably lower frequency than via female germline transmission, our results demonstrate conclusively that the mouse male germline can successfully package an exogenous and aneuploid 42 MB human chromosome into protamines to generate reproductively active sperm.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the breeding and FISH data presented.

claim: There were neither qualitative nor quantitative differences in the locations of transcription initiation in endoderm-derived livers from male and female germline-derived Tc1 mice.
source: Across the entire human chromosome, we observed neither qualitative nor quantitative differences in the locations of transcription initiation in endoderm-derived livers from male and female germline-derived Tc1 mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on H3K4me3 ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The stability of the eventual intensity of transcription initiation was found at all unidirectional and bidirectional promoters, regardless of their proximal or distal positioning relative to coding and noncoding genes.
source: The stability of the eventual intensity of transcription initiation was found at all unidirectional and bidirectional promoters, regardless of their proximal or distal positioning relative to coding and noncoding genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on H3K4me3 ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In all profiled tissues, the large-scale remodelling caused by male germline passage of the human chromosome resulted in transcription initiation indistinguishable from female germline-derived HsChr21.
source: In all profiled tissues, the large-scale remodelling caused by male germline passage of the human chromosome resulted in transcription initiation indistinguishable from female germline-derived HsChr21 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on H3K4me3 ChIP-Seq data across multiple tissues shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The process of chromatin decondensation after fertilization does not distort the transcriptional deployment of the aneuploid human chromosome during mouse embryogenesis.
source: These results strongly argue that the process of chromatin decondensation (and complete rebuild by the mouse machinery) after fertilization does not distort the transcriptional deployment of the aneuploid human chromosome during mouse embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcription initiation data across multiple tissues.

claim: The mouse nuclear environment unmasks a number of human- and primate-specific repetitive elements across chromosome 21 passaged through the female germline.
source: Our previous comparisons between Tc1 mice and humans in liver showed that the mouse nuclear environment unmasks a number of human- and primate-specific repetitive elements across chromosome 21 passaged through the female germline (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on previous work cited as Ward et al., 2013.

claim: The previously-reported mouse-specific transcription initiation events located at human repeat elements were accurately regenerated when the aneuploid human chromosome was passed through the male germline.
source: However, the previously-reported mouse-specific transcription initiation events located at human repeat elements were accurately regenerated when the aneuploid human chromosome was passed through the male germline (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on differential binding analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Promoter and enhancer activity is highly correlated between male and female germline-derived mice (r2 = 0.99 and 0.96, respectively).
source: Promoter and enhancer activity is highly correlated between male and female germline-derived mice (r2 = 0.99 and 0.96, respectively) with no significantly differentially bound sites on chromosome 21 (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq data for H3K4me3 and H3K27ac shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: There are no significantly differentially bound sites on chromosome 21 for H3K4me3 and H3K27ac between male and female germline-derived mice.
source: Promoter and enhancer activity is highly correlated between male and female germline-derived mice (r2 = 0.99 and 0.96, respectively) with no significantly differentially bound sites on chromosome 21 (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on differential binding analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: DNA methylation in adult somatic tissues converges on the same molecular phenotype between male and female germline-derived mice (r2 = 0.97).
source: As with the chromatin marks above, DNA methylation in adult somatic tissues converges on the same molecular phenotype (r2 = 0.97) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on BioCAP-sequencing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The correlation in genomic occupancy between male and female germline-derived mice for CEBPA and HNF4A was r2 = 0.72–0.83.
source: Unsurprisingly, the correlation in genomic occupancy between male and female germline-derived mice for two liver-specific transcription factors (CEBPA and HNF4A) and Pol II were slightly noisier (r2 = 0.72–0.83) (Stefflova et al., 2013); nevertheless, almost no sites were identified reliably as differentially bound (Figure 6D-F).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-Seq data for CEBPA and HNF4A shown in Figure 6D and 6E, with citation to Stefflova et al., 2013.

claim: Almost no sites were identified reliably as differentially bound for CEBPA, HNF4A, and Pol II between male and female germline-derived mice.
source: Unsurprisingly, the correlation in genomic occupancy between male and female germline-derived mice for two liver-specific transcription factors (CEBPA and HNF4A) and Pol II were slightly noisier (r2 = 0.72–0.83) (Stefflova et al., 2013); nevertheless, almost no sites were identified reliably as differentially bound (Figure 6D-F).
evidence: This is based on differential binding analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: The transcriptome shows exceptionally high correlation between livers of Tc1 female- and male-derived offspring (r2 = 0.97), with no genes identified as differentially expressed.
source: Notably, the modest differences observed in polymerase occupancy do not impact the transcriptome, which shows exceptionally high correlation between livers of Tc1 female- and male-derived offspring (r2 = 0.97), with no genes identified as differentially expressed (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Despite the massive epigenetic remodelling and chromatin condensation associated with male germline transmission, human chromosome 21 is accurately deployed in multiple diverse tissues during development by the mouse epigenetic machinery.
source: Overall, despite the massive epigenetic remodelling and chromatin condensation associated with male germline transmission, human chromosome 21 is accurately deployed in multiple diverse tissues during development by the mouse epigenetic machinery.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the epigenetic profiling data presented.

claim: Aneuploid female mice that carry large amounts of exogenous DNA are fertile and can pass aneuploid DNA on to their offspring.
source: Aneuploid female mice that carry large amounts of exogenous DNA are fertile and can pass aneuploid DNA on to their offspring; however, aneuploid male mice have strongly suppressed fertility and are often entirely sterile (Co et al., 2000; Hernandez and Fisher, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Co et al., 2000 and Hernandez and Fisher, 1999.

claim: Aneuploid male mice have strongly suppressed fertility and are often entirely sterile.
source: Aneuploid female mice that carry large amounts of exogenous DNA are fertile and can pass aneuploid DNA on to their offspring; however, aneuploid male mice have strongly suppressed fertility and are often entirely sterile (Co et al., 2000; Hernandez and Fisher, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Co et al., 2000 and Hernandez and Fisher, 1999.

claim: In more than 50% of the cases, human chromosome 21 is incorporated into the large γH2AFX domain together with X and Y chromosome to mask their incomplete synapsis, resulting in transcriptional silencing.
source: In more than 50% of the cases, human chromosome 21 is incorporated into the large γH2AFX domain together with X and Y chromosome to mask their incomplete synapsis, resulting in transcriptional silencing (Handel, 2004).
evidence: This is based on previous work cited as Mahadevaiah et al., 2008 and Handel, 2004.

claim: The presence of human chromosome 21 did not lead to increased pachytene apoptosis in epithelial stage IV tubules.
source: However, independent of whether human chromosome 21 would be unsynapsed and in proximity to the XY body or self-synapsed and located away from XY, the presence of human chromosome 21 did not lead to increased pachytene apoptosis in epithelial stage IV tubules (Mahadevaiah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on previous work cited as Mahadevaiah et al., 2008.

claim: The largest successful and stable germline transmission of human DNA via mouse sperm was of a circularized 5–10 megabase human artificial chromosome.
source: To date, the largest successful and stable germline transmission of human DNA via mouse sperm was of a circularized 5–10 megabase human artificial chromosome (Voet et al., 2001); a linearized version of this same artificial chromosome containing short telomeres can also be passaged via sperm (Weuts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Voet et al., 2001 and Weuts et al., 2012.

claim: A linearized version of a human artificial chromosome containing short telomeres can be passaged via sperm.
source: To date, the largest successful and stable germline transmission of human DNA via mouse sperm was of a circularized 5–10 megabase human artificial chromosome (Voet et al., 2001); a linearized version of this same artificial chromosome containing short telomeres can also be passaged via sperm (Weuts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weuts et al., 2012.

claim: The majority of Tc1 males tested in this study were able to produce viable aneuploid offspring, albeit at lower frequencies.
source: Nevertheless, despite frequent spermatogenic arrest at metaphase I leading to increased apoptosis, the majority of Tc1 males tested in this study were able to produce viable aneuploid offspring, albeit at lower frequencies.
evidence: This is based on breeding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The observed lower transmission rate of HsChr21 cannot be fully accounted for by the reduced number of HsChr21 positive cells produced during male meiosis.
source: The observed lower transmission rate of HsChr21, however, cannot be fully accounted for by the reduced number of HsChr21 positive cells produced during male meiosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the percentage of HsChr21-positive spermatids (34%) with the transmission rate (11%).

claim: Failures in transmission are likely to occur during sperm maturation, at fertilization or during early embryonic development.
source: This indicates that failures are likely to occur further downstream, i.e. during sperm maturation, at fertilization or during early embryonic development, eventually resulting in only ~ 11% aneuploid offspring.
evidence: This is speculation based on the discrepancy between the percentage of HsChr21-positive spermatids and the transmission rate.

claim: The percentage of aneuploid cells produced via male meiosis (34%) is strikingly similar to the percentage of aneuploid offspring generated via female germline transmission.
source: While female meiosis is more error-prone than male meiosis due to weaker checkpoint mechanisms (Morelli and Cohen, 2005), the percentage of aneuploid cells produced via male meiosis (34%) is strikingly similar to the percentage of aneuploid offspring generated via female germline transmission.
evidence: This is a comparison based on data presented in the manuscript and cited reference to Morelli and Cohen, 2005.

claim: Attempts to establish the Tc1 chromosome on three different inbred genetic backgrounds led to a complete loss of HsChr21 over only a few generations.
source: Attempts to establish the Tc1 chromosome on three different inbred genetic backgrounds led to a complete loss of HsChr21 over only a few generations (O'Doherty et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on previous work cited as O'Doherty et al., 2005.

claim: The loss of the human chromosome was independent of the sex of the transmitting parent.
source: The loss of the human chromosome was independent of the sex of the transmitting parent, and stable transmission was only observed when Tc1 mice were crossed with F1 hybrids between BL6 and 129S8 mice.
evidence: This is based on observations from breeding experiments.

claim: Stable transmission of HsChr21 was only observed when Tc1 mice were crossed with F1 hybrids between BL6 and 129S8 mice.
source: The loss of the human chromosome was independent of the sex of the transmitting parent, and stable transmission was only observed when Tc1 mice were crossed with F1 hybrids between BL6 and 129S8 mice.
evidence: This is based on observations from breeding experiments.

claim: The Tc1 mouse recapitulates many clinical features of human trisomy 21.
source: The Tc1 mouse has long been an elegant model of human Down syndrome that recapitulates many clinical features of human trisomy 21 (O'Doherty et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to O'Doherty et al., 2005.

claim: Down syndrome, especially when paternally inherited, exhibits a strong sex bias (up to a 3.5 male/female ratio).
source: Down syndrome, especially when paternally inherited, exhibits a strong sex bias (up to a 3.5 male/female ratio), which has been attributed to a preference of the extra chromosome to segregate with the Y chromosome (Hassold et al., 1984; Nicolaidis and Petersen, 1998; Petersen et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hassold et al., 1984; Nicolaidis and Petersen, 1998; and Petersen et al., 1993.

claim: No sex bias was observed amongst aneuploid offspring from either female or male germline transmission (1.0 and 1.1, respectively).
source: In contrast, however, we did not observe a sex bias amongst aneuploid offspring from either female or male germline transmission (1.0 and 1.1, respectively), possibly reflecting interspecies differences in segregation patterns.
evidence: This is based on breeding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No additional repeat elements appeared to be transcriptionally activated in somatic tissues following male germline transmission.
source: However, no additional repeat elements appeared to be transcriptionally activated in somatic tissues following male germline transmission.
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcription initiation at repeat elements.

claim: The radically differing developmental dynamics of male- versus female-germline passage of the aneuploid chromosome can result in indistinguishable transcriptional and regulatory phenotypes.
source: Our results reveal the remarkable insight that mouse male meiosis can tolerate the presence of an aneuploid 42 MB human chromosome to generate viable sperm. The radically differing developmental dynamics of male- versus female-germline passage of this aneuploid chromosome can nevertheless result in indistinguishable transcriptional and regulatory phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the manuscript.
